The Burnham administration scrapped the digital ID scheme introduced by the previous government, which had faced significant backlash and a petition signed by nearly 3 million citizens concerned about surveillance.

Public feedback successfully influenced government policy, demonstrating that democratic mechanisms can still function to halt invasive state programs.

This is a WHO/WHY error; the government shifted from a top-down mandate to a responsive stance, acknowledging the public as the primary stakeholder rather than a resource to be managed.

By prioritizing public feedback over a pre-existing bureaucratic mandate, the government moved from a coercive power structure to one that empowers citizens, effectively defusing a major source of social friction.
